audio.t: Good afternoon, everyone. Since midterm grades were posted yesterday, I've received a lot of emails, so I'd like to take a few minutes to explain how office hours work in this course. First, my regular hours are Monday and Wednesday from three to four thirty, in room two fifteen of the Science Building. You don't need an appointment for those times. If you can't make it, you can book a fifteen-minute online slot through the course website.

Second, please come prepared. Office hours are most useful when you bring specific questions. Instead of saying, I don't understand chapter five, try to point to the exact problem or step where you got lost. Also, bring your notes and any work you've already done. That way, I can see how you're thinking, not just where you ended up.

Finally, a word about grades. I'm happy to go over your midterm with you, but I can't change any scores during office hours. If you believe a question was graded incorrectly, write a short explanation and submit it to Professor Chang within one week.

questions.explain: 開頭說昨天公布期中成績後收到很多信，所以要說明 office hours 怎麼運作，故選 B。A 地點並未改變；C 未提及教授不在。

passage: Every week, teaching assistants on our campus spend about three hours in their offices waiting for students. According to a survey conducted by the Student Learning Center last month, many of them wait alone. Of the 1,200 undergraduates who responded, only 23 percent said they had attended office hours at least once this semester.

The reasons students gave were surprisingly consistent. Nearly half said the times clashed with their other classes or part-time jobs. Another common answer was embarrassment. "I don't want the TA to think I'm not smart enough," one second-year engineering student explained. Others said they were unsure what office hours were for, believing they were only meant for students who were failing.

Meanwhile, TAs report the opposite problem in their inboxes. Wang Yi-Chen, a graduate student who assists in two accounting courses, receives up to forty emails a week. "Many of these questions would take two minutes to answer in person but twenty minutes to explain in writing," she said.

To close this gap, the Learning Center will launch a pilot program next semester. Selected courses will offer evening drop-in sessions in the library, as well as small group sessions in which several students work through problems together. The center also plans to send short videos to first-year students showing what happens during a typical visit. Instructors who want their courses to join the program can apply through the center by December 15.
"Office hours are not a punishment," said center director Dr. Lisa Huang. "They are one of the most effective learning tools we have, and they're already included in your tuition."
